title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a data-sourcing decision made before deployment. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack indicates it scraped platforms including YouTube, Deezer, and Genius. No licensing or rights-clearance step was applied to that training corpus. The system was then deployed publicly in a way that allowed outputs to reproduce recognizable portions of specific copyrighted recordings, which is where the sourcing failure became a product liability.

This is a case of a system deployed outside the conditions under which its training data was legally permissible to use. The failure point was upstream of the model itself, in the data-collection pipeline, and it would have required rights clearance, filtering by license status, or both before training began. A human review of outputs alone would not have been sufficient to catch it, because the problem was baked into the weights before any output was generated.

What is established is that multiple lawsuits have been filed, that a German court ruled against Suno in GEMA's case, that Warner Music settled its suit and formed a partnership with Suno, and that Universal Music settled with Udio. What is not established is the full legal outcome in the United States proceedings, and the allegations of deliberate concealment of training data sources remain claims in litigation rather than proven findings.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno. The labels accuse both companies of scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits claim the companies have deliberately concealed which songs they used for training and that both services can directly reproduce sections of famous songs. The record labels submitted a comprehensive list of thousands of copyrighted works they believe were scraped, featuring artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Coldplay, and many others.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate versions of famous songs by using specific prompts describing characteristics like decade, genre, and artist style. For example, they generated outputs matching Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, where the companies are based. Both AI companies previously claimed their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use, a position the labels dispute.
